title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about being critical at university: what the word really means and how to do it. By the end you will be able to explain what being critical is, tell active engagement with a source from passive, and use the basic language of criticality - analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement.

These are not abstract study skills. 'Be more critical' is one of the most common things tutors write on student work, in every subject. Knowing what it asks, and having the habits and the words to do it, changes how you read, how you write, and the marks your work earns.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what it means to be critical at university
distinguish active from passive engagement with academic sources
use the basic language of criticality to describe critical thinking.

title: In real academic practice
body: Being critical is the habit academic work is built on. Every essay that asks you to discuss or evaluate, every seminar where views are weighed, every piece of reading you are expected to question rather than accept, draws on the same mindset. Build it now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the judgement that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what being critical means: the mindset behind the word. Second, active versus passive engagement: what that mindset looks like when you read a source. Third, the language of criticality: the words that name each critical move. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: Orientation
body: When a tutor writes 'be more critical' on your work, it can feel like a vague instruction. It does not mean find fault or be negative. Being critical is a way of approaching what you read and think - a mindset that confident, self-directed students bring to everything they study. This lesson looks at what that mindset is, so the instruction stops being vague and starts being something you can actually do.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and 'being critical' may be new as something to aim for deliberately. At this stage you are not expected to produce sharp critiques of expert work. The aim is to recognise critical thinking when you see it and understand the mindset behind it - the foundation you will build on as you progress.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that being critical is a mindset, not a skill switched on and off
recognise critical thought in a worked example of a student's approach
identify what being critical asks of you when you read a source in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
'Being critical' is not a switch you flick on for an essay and off again. It is a mindset - a way of thinking and acting that runs through how a successful, self-directed student reads, questions and uses ideas. To be critical is to treat what you read as something to weigh and interrogate, not simply to accept and repeat.

This matters because university rewards what you can do with ideas - judge them, connect them, question them - far more than how many you can recall. This lesson is about what that mindset is; the lessons that follow are about how you use it when you read and write.

title: Summary
body: Being critical at university is a mindset, not a switch or a fault-finding exercise: it means bringing a questioning, weighing approach to everything you read and write. You can now explain what that mindset is and recognise it in how a student approaches a source. The next lessons turn the mindset into practice - how you engage with sources actively, and the language that describes critical thinking.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that being critical is a mindset. This lesson is about what that mindset looks like in action when you sit down with a source. The difference between a passive reader and an active one is not how much they read, but what they do with it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to take apart an expert's argument yet. The aim here is to notice the difference between reading that just takes a source in and reading that works with it, and to try a few active moves of your own.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: tell active engagement with a source apart from passive engagement
give an example of opening up the discourse around a source
choose an active move to make when a source in {{context}} states something as settled.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Passive reading takes a source at face value: you read it, note what it says, and move on, treating the author's conclusion as a fact to collect. Active reading engages with the source: you ask what it is claiming, what it rests on, and how it fits with other things you have read, treating the conclusion as one position among others.

The move that matters is opening up the discourse. Rather than accepting a single source as the last word, you treat it as one voice in a conversation your subject is having, and you join that conversation by asking questions of it. This is the habit that turns the critical mindset into real work.

title: Summary
body: Being critical becomes real work when you engage with a source actively rather than passively: questioning its claim, testing what it rests on, and opening up the discourse by bringing in other voices. You can now tell active engagement from passive, and choose an active move when a source sounds settled. The next lesson gives you the language to describe these moves precisely.

title: Orientation
body: You have seen that being critical is a mindset, and what it looks like to engage with a source actively. This lesson gives you the words for it. Criticality has its own vocabulary, such as analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement, and knowing what each word means helps you do the thing it names and recognise when a tutor is asking for it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to use these words to sound clever. The aim is to understand what each one actually asks you to do, so that when an assignment says analyse or evaluate, you know the kind of thinking it wants.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use the basic language of criticality (analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement) correctly
tell a judgement apart from a description
match a critical move in {{context}} to the word that names it.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Criticality has a working vocabulary, and each word names a different move. Analysis means breaking something into parts to see how it works. Evaluation means weighing how good or well-supported something is. Synthesis means drawing several sources or ideas together into a view of your own. Judgement means reaching a reasoned position and being able to say why.

These words matter because assignments use them as instructions. Analyse, evaluate and discuss are not interchangeable: each asks for a particular kind of thinking. Knowing the language lets you give a tutor what they are actually asking for, and lets you name what you are doing when you read.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a recent assignment brief in your subject. Which of the four words (analyse, evaluate, synthesise, judge) did it ask for, and did you do that move?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Criticality has a working vocabulary: analysis breaks things down, evaluation weighs them, synthesis draws them together, and judgement reaches a reasoned position. You can now use these words correctly, tell a judgement apart from a description, and name the critical move an assignment is asking for. With the mindset, the active habits and the language in place, you are ready to be critical on purpose.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Being critical is no longer a vague instruction: it is a mindset you can describe and begin to use. You can explain what being critical means - a questioning, weighing habit rather than fault-finding or a switch. You can tell active engagement with a source from passive, and open up the discourse around what you read. And you have the language of criticality - analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement - to name each move. body: From here, being critical is something you practise in every module. Each time a brief says analyse or evaluate, each source you weigh rather than accept, each judgement you reach with reasons, is the mindset at work. It is also what professional life rewards: the ability to question, weigh evidence and decide with reasons travels well beyond your degree.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four everyday ideas about what 'being critical' really means. Turn each card to see past the common misunderstanding.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: Being critical does not mean attacking a source or finding fault. It means weighing an idea carefully - asking how well it is supported and where it holds or breaks - rather than dismissing it or simply praising it.

You cannot be critical only when an essay is marked. It is a habit you bring to all your reading and thinking: noticing claims, asking what they rest on, and staying curious about how you know what you know.

A passive reader takes a source at face value and moves on. A critical reader engages - questioning the argument, testing it against other ideas, and deciding what to make of it. The source is the same; what you do with it differs.

Being critical is characteristic of a confident, self-regulating student - someone who does not wait to be told what to think, but works out, with reasons, what to think for themselves. That is the mindset this course helps you build.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students given the same journal article to use in an essay.

{{learner-a}} reads the article, notes that it supports the essay's point, and quotes it as evidence. The source has been found and used. But {{learner-a}} has taken it at face value - accepting the claim because it is published, without asking how the author reached it or whether others see it differently. This is passive reading.

{{learner-b}} reads the same article and keeps asking questions. What is the author actually claiming? What evidence is it built on? Who might disagree, and why? {{learner-b}} still uses the article, but now as one voice in a debate - weighed, placed, and drawn on with judgement. This is being critical.

Both students found the same source. Only {{learner-b}} brought the critical mindset to it, turning a quotation into a judgement.

title: Critical habits
body: These habits turn the critical mindset into something you do. Try them on your next piece of reading.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I asked what this source is actually claiming, in my own words?
Have I asked what evidence the claim rests on?
Have I asked who might disagree, and why?
Have I checked the idea against something else I have read?
Have I decided what I make of it, rather than just repeating it?
Have I noticed when I am accepting a source simply because it is published?

title: Explore the concept
body: Four shifts that turn passive reading into active reading. Turn each card to see the move.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Take it in, or ask of it?
_items.body: A passive reader notes what a source says. An active reader asks what it is claiming and why that matters. Same page, different work: the active reader leaves with questions, not just notes.

_items.title: One source, or a conversation?
_items.body: Passive reading treats a source as the final word. Active reading treats it as one voice in your subject's ongoing conversation. Opening up that conversation, by asking who else has a view, is the heart of being active.

_items.title: Accept it, or test it?
_items.body: When a source states something as settled, a passive reader accepts it. An active reader tests it: what evidence is behind this, and does everyone in the field agree? That testing is not rudeness; it is how knowledge is checked.

_items.title: Store it, or connect it?
_items.body: Passive reading stores a fact on its own. Active reading connects it: how does this fit with last week's reading, or with another source that says something different? Connections are where understanding is built.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students read the same textbook passage, which states a claim as though it were settled fact.

{{learner-a}} reads the passage, accepts the claim, and writes it into their notes as a fact to use later. The reading is done and the point is captured. But {{learner-a}} has taken the author's word for it, with no sense of where the claim came from or whether anyone sees it differently. This is passive engagement.

{{learner-b}} reads the same passage and pauses on the word that makes it sound settled. Is this really agreed? {{learner-b}} checks what the claim rests on, looks for a second source, and finds the field is still debating it. The claim goes into the notes, but now as a position to weigh, not a fact to repeat. This is active engagement: the discourse has been opened up.

Both students read the passage. Only {{learner-b}} treated it as something to question rather than simply to accept.

Have I asked what evidence the claim is built on?
Have I looked for a second source that sees it differently?

Have I connected this source to something else I have read?
Have I noted a question to raise, rather than only a fact to keep?

_incorrect.final: Active engagement questions the claim, tests it, and connects it to other reading. Careful notes, extra re-reads and accurate quotes are all still passive if the source is treated as the last word.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four words that name the moves of critical thinking. Turn each card to see what it asks you to do.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that word.

_items.title: Analysis
_items.body: Analysis means breaking something down to see how it works: its parts, how they fit, what it is made of. When you analyse an argument, you separate the claim from the evidence and the assumptions, rather than taking it as one lump.

_items.title: Evaluation
_items.body: Evaluation means weighing: how strong is this, how well supported, how convincing compared with the alternatives? To evaluate is to judge quality with reasons, not just to say whether you liked it.

_items.title: Synthesis
_items.body: Synthesis means drawing several sources or ideas together into something new: a view of your own that none of the sources stated on its own. It is the opposite of summarising one source at a time.

_items.title: Judgement
_items.body: Judgement means reaching a reasoned position and being able to defend it. A judgement is more than a description of what a source says: it is your considered view of what it is worth or what it means, with reasons attached.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are asked to write about the same study for a seminar.

{{learner-a}} writes: the study found that the effect was large, and the authors concluded it was important. This is accurate, and it is a description: it reports what the source says, faithfully, but adds nothing of the student's own. The reader learns what the study claimed, not what to make of it.

{{learner-b}} writes: the study reports a large effect, but the sample was small and drawn from one setting, so its claim to importance is not yet secure. This is a judgement: it still reports the study, but it weighs the evidence and reaches a reasoned position about how far to trust the claim.

Both students understood the study. Only {{learner-b}} moved from describing it to judging it, the step the language of criticality is built to name.

title: Naming the move
body: Use these questions to check which critical move you are making, and whether you are describing or judging.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: When I broke the argument into claim, evidence and assumptions, was I analysing?
When I weighed how well-supported a claim was, was I evaluating?
When I pulled several sources into a view of my own, was I synthesising?
When I reached a reasoned position and gave my reasons, was I judging?
Have I checked whether my sentence describes the source or judges it?
When an assignment says analyse or evaluate, have I done the move the word names?

title: Formative check: the language of criticality
displayTitle: Which of these is the best description of what evaluation asks you to do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option best describes what evaluation asks you to do?

_items.text: Break an idea into its parts to see how it is put together.
_items.feedback: That is analysis, not evaluation.

_items.text: Weigh how strong or well-supported something is, with reasons.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evaluation is weighing quality, with reasons.

_items.text: Summarise accurately what a single source says.
_items.feedback: That is description or summary, not evaluation.

_items.text: Draw several sources together into a view of your own.
_items.feedback: That is synthesis, not evaluation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Evaluation means weighing how strong or well-supported something is, with reasons.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Evaluation is about weighing quality; the other options name analysis, summary or synthesis.
_incorrect.final: Evaluation means weighing how strong or well-supported something is, with reasons. Breaking down is analysis, reporting is description, and combining is synthesis.

title: Formative check: judgement versus description
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's sentence a judgement rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's sentence a judgement?

_items.text: It weighed the evidence and reached a reasoned position about the claim.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing the evidence and taking a reasoned position is what makes it a judgement.

_items.text: It reported the study's findings more accurately.
_items.feedback: Accurate reporting is description; a judgement goes beyond reporting.

_items.text: It was longer than the first student's sentence.
_items.feedback: Length does not make a judgement; weighing and reasoning do.

_items.text: It quoted the authors' own conclusion.
_items.feedback: Quoting the authors still reports their view rather than reaching your own.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second sentence weighed the evidence and reached a reasoned position, which is a judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the sentence DID beyond reporting, that is, weighing and taking a position.
_incorrect.final: The second sentence was a judgement because it weighed the evidence and reached a reasoned position. Accurate reporting, extra length or a quotation are all still description.

title: Formative check: naming the move
displayTitle: While studying {{context}}, you draw three sources together into a view none of them stated on its own. Which word names what you have done?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which word names drawing several sources into a new view?

_items.text: Synthesis.
_items.feedback: Yes. Combining several sources into a new view of your own is synthesis.

_items.text: Analysis.
_items.feedback: Analysis breaks one thing into parts; it does not combine sources into a new view.

_items.text: Description.
_items.feedback: Description reports what a source says; it does not build a new view.

_items.text: Evaluation.
_items.feedback: Evaluation weighs quality; here you are combining sources, which is synthesis.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Drawing several sources into a view of your own is synthesis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. You combined several sources into something new; which of the four words names that?
_incorrect.final: Combining several sources into a view none stated on its own is synthesis. Analysis breaks down, description reports, and evaluation weighs.

body: When a tutor writes 'be more critical' on your essay, what are they mainly asking for?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is a tutor mainly asking for when they write be more critical?

_items.text: That you bring a questioning, weighing mindset to the material.
_items.feedback: Yes. Being critical is a mindset you apply to the material.

_items.text: That you find fault with every source you cite.
_items.feedback: Being critical is not fault-finding; it is weighing, not attacking.

_items.text: That you write more and cite more sources.
_items.feedback: More words and more sources are not criticality.

_items.text: That you add a critical paragraph at the end.
_items.feedback: It is a habit throughout, not a bolt-on paragraph.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Being critical means bringing a questioning, weighing mindset to the material.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the mindset the instruction is really asking for.

body: Which of these best shows the critical mindset rather than a passive one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best shows the critical mindset rather than a passive one?

_items.text: Asking what a claim rests on and whether others in the field disagree.
_items.feedback: Yes. Questioning and weighing is the critical mindset.

_items.text: Accepting a claim because it appears in a published source.
_items.feedback: Accepting because it is published is the passive approach.

_items.text: Highlighting the key sentences to memorise them.
_items.feedback: Highlighting to memorise does not weigh the claim.

_items.text: Copying the author's conclusion into your notes.
_items.feedback: Copying reproduces the claim rather than questioning it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Asking what a claim rests on, and who might disagree, is the critical mindset in action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that questions and weighs the claim.

body: A student reads a source, accepts its claim, and writes it into their notes as a fact. This is an example of engaging with the source...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student accepts a source's claim and notes it as fact. This engagement is...

_items.text: passively.
_items.feedback: Yes. Taking a claim at face value is passive engagement.

_items.text: actively.
_items.feedback: Active engagement would question and test the claim, not just accept it.

_items.text: critically.
_items.feedback: Accepting without questioning is the opposite of critical.

_items.text: analytically.
_items.feedback: No analysis has taken place; the claim was simply accepted.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Accepting a claim at face value is passive engagement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Did the student question the claim, or simply accept it?

body: What does it mean to open up the discourse around a source?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to open up the discourse around a source?

_items.text: To treat it as one voice in a debate and bring in other views.
_items.feedback: Yes. That turns a single source into a conversation.

_items.text: To read it several times until you agree with it.
_items.feedback: Re-reading does not open a discourse; bringing in other voices does.

_items.text: To accept its conclusion because it is on the reading list.
_items.feedback: That accepts a single source as the last word.

_items.text: To summarise it as accurately as possible.
_items.feedback: Accurate summary still treats the one source as final.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Opening up the discourse means treating a source as one voice among others.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that brings in other views.

body: Weighing how strong or well-supported a claim is, with reasons, is which move of criticality?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Weighing how well-supported a claim is, with reasons, is which move?

_items.text: Evaluation.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evaluation is weighing quality, with reasons.

_items.text: Analysis.
_items.feedback: Analysis breaks something into parts; it does not weigh quality.

_items.text: Description.
_items.feedback: Description reports; it does not weigh.

_items.text: Synthesis.
_items.feedback: Synthesis combines sources; it does not weigh one claim.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing quality with reasons is evaluation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which word names weighing how well-supported something is?

body: You draw three sources together into a view of your own that none of them stated alone. Which word names what you have done?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Drawing several sources into a new view of your own is which move?

_items.text: Synthesis.
_items.feedback: Yes. Combining sources into a new view is synthesis.

_items.text: Evaluation.
_items.feedback: Evaluation weighs; here you combined sources.

_items.text: Description.
_items.feedback: Description reports a source; it does not build a new view.

_items.text: Analysis.
_items.feedback: Analysis breaks one thing down; it does not combine sources.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Combining several sources into a view of your own is synthesis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which word names combining sources into something new?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what being critical means as a mindset, how to engage with a source actively rather than passively, and the language that names each critical move. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to produce polished critiques of expert work. The aim is to see being critical as one joined-up practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it carries on past this course into every subject you study.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how the critical mindset, active engagement and the language of criticality connect as one practice
show the whole critical practice at work in a worked example of a student's approach to a source
plan one way to be critical on purpose when you read and write in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: Being critical on purpose is the three strands working as one. You bring the questioning mindset to a source, you engage with it actively rather than accepting it, and you use the language of criticality to name and sharpen each move. The mindset is why you do it, active engagement is how you do it, and the language lets you do it precisely and say what you are doing.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, being critical is one thing you do, not three. Faced with a source, you choose to question it, you engage with its claims and evidence, and you name and sharpen each move with the language of criticality. Done together, in any subject, these turn reading into a reasoned judgement of your own.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one piece of reading or writing coming up in your studies. How will you bring the mindset, active engagement and the language together on it, and when?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Being critical is most useful when the three strands work as one. You bring the questioning mindset, engage with a source actively, and use the language to name each move and reach a judgement. It is the whole practice, not any single part, that changes how you read and write.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The steps as one process
body: Being critical on purpose runs as one process, from a questioning approach to a reasoned judgement. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Question
_items.body: Bring a questioning mindset to the source rather than accepting it at face value.

_items.title: Engage
_items.body: Engage with it actively, asking what it claims, what it rests on and who might disagree.

_items.title: Name moves
_items.body: Name the moves you are making, such as analysing the argument or evaluating the evidence.

_items.title: Judge
_items.body: Reach a reasoned judgement you can defend, and carry it into your writing.

title: Worked example
body: Two students read the same source for an assignment. One has the critical words but only skims, accepting the claim and quoting it. The other brings all three strands together: she questions the claim, weighs its evidence against another source, names the moves as analysis and evaluation, and reaches a judgement of her own. Her work is stronger, because being critical became one practice rather than three separate things.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to be critical on purpose
body: Use these to bring the mindset, the active habits and the language together on your next piece of reading.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I chosen to question this source rather than take it at face value?
Have I asked what it claims, what it rests on, and who might disagree?
Have I named the move I am making, such as analysis, evaluation or synthesis?
Have I reached a judgement of my own, with reasons, rather than just a description?
Have I carried that judgement into what I write or say?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat being critical as one practice rather than three separate things?
body: Why is it more useful to treat being critical as one practice rather than three separate things?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat being critical as one practice rather than three separate things?

_items.text: Because the three work together: the mindset sets you questioning, active engagement does the questioning, and the language names each move.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each strand needs the others to do real critical work.

_items.text: Because knowing the four critical words is enough on its own to be critical.
_items.feedback: The words only help once you bring the mindset and engage with a source.

_items.text: Because being critical is really just finding fault, so the parts do not matter.
_items.feedback: Being critical is not fault-finding, and the three parts very much matter.

_items.text: Because you only need the mindset, and the rest looks after itself.
_items.feedback: The mindset alone is not enough. You still have to engage and name the moves.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The mindset, active engagement and the language are one joined-up practice, each part leaning on the others.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what each strand adds, and why one on its own is not enough.

displayTitle: A student reads a source, questions what it claims, weighs the evidence against another source, and reaches a reasoned judgement of her own. What does this show?
body: A student reads a source, questions what it claims, weighs the evidence against another source, and reaches a reasoned judgement of her own. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reads a source, questions what it claims, weighs the evidence against another source, and reaches a reasoned judgement of her own. What does this show?

_items.text: The whole critical practice at work: the mindset, active engagement, and the language of weighing and judging together.
_items.feedback: Yes. She brought the mindset, engaged actively, and judged with reasons, all in one go.

_items.text: Passive reading, because she used a source in her work.
_items.feedback: Using a source is not passive in itself. She questioned and judged it.

_items.text: Only analysis, because she broke the argument into parts.
_items.feedback: She did more than analyse. She also weighed the evidence and reached a judgement.

_items.text: Fault-finding, because she disagreed with the source.
_items.feedback: Weighing a source and judging it with reasons is not the same as fault-finding.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Questioning, weighing against another source, and judging with reasons is the whole practice working as one.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at everything she did, not just one move.

_items.feedback: Accepting a source because it is set reading is the passive habit to avoid.

_items.text: Only question sources you already disagree with, and accept the rest.
_items.feedback: Being critical means weighing every source, not only the ones you doubt.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Questioning, engaging, naming the move and judging with reasons is the whole practice at work in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that brings the mindset, active engagement and the language together.
